newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's PM calls for foreign investments.
newsitem.headline: Romania's PM calls for foreign investments.

text.p: Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea urged foreign investors on Tuesday to take another look at Romania, saying capital inflows were crucial for the reforms launched by his coalition government.

"Our reform programme depends essentially on attracting foreign investments," Ciorbea told Western businessmen at a Bucharest conference held to highlight investment opportunities in the ex-communist country.
Ciorbea said that within the next two months his government would bring in or revise up to 80 laws in order to draw much- needed direct and portfolio investments from the West.

Romania, which has attracted only little over $2.0 billion in foreign capital since the 1989 fall of communism, is keen to bridge the economic gap separating it from more developed East Europeans Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary.

Two weeks ago the new government announced radical reforms, including faster privatisation and restructuring of communist-era industries, in exchange for renewed credits from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
The government has pledged to cut monthly inflation, now running at around 14.0 percent, to some 2.5 percent by the end of 1997, as well as to slash bulging deficits.

Last month parliament's upper Senate passed a bill granting foreigners the right to buy land in Romania. The bill has yet to clear the lower Chamber of Deputies, where Ciorbea's centrist coalition government has a comfortable majority.

"We plan to allow foreign banks to acquire around 90 to 95 percent of Romanian (state) banks' capital and to develop capital markets," said Ciorbea, whose centrists ousted ex-communists in elections last November.

The former ruling leftists failed in their promises to privatise two of the six state-run banks in 1995. Last year, the conservatives who dominated the old parliament had twice thrown out a long-awaited bank selloff bill, a plank under loan accords with international lenders.
Ciorbea invited foreign companies to buy stakes in state utilities, communications and oil plants up for privatisation: "If you are interested to invest in such areas you're welcome."

The government plans to launch the privatisation of state Romtelecom RA telephone company later this year. It also wants to restructure and privatise another 20 utilities, including electricity authority Renel RA.
Ciorbea vowed to cut red tape, which he said had been often cited as an "insurmountable obstacle" by foreign investors.

Foreign investments in Romania, eastern Europe's second-largest market after Poland, are about a tenth of what neighbouring Hungary has attracted over the past seven years. Local economists say that Romania needs at least a $1.0 billion a year in foreign capital inflows. -- Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264
